ACT TO PROVIDE FOR THE CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in conversations with the Liberal critic and the Minister of Labour I think the Labour Minister knows that we will not agree to passage of all stages on Monday.
We have agreed, in order for the parties to get together today, Saturday and Sunday, that we would waive the usual notice and would allow the second reading debate to start on Monday. If the parties have not come to agreement or if we are in a situation where the parties come to us and say that they need more time to settle the dispute, we may again hold off the actual
commencement of this debate. But there is no way that we would agree to passage in all stages on Monday of a bill that we have not seen. That just cannot be done.
The reason we are allowing or are willing to allow that we would start second reading on Monday is that we do not want any of the parties to see the legislation. We want them to be spending their time, their efforts, their emotions, their thoughts on negotiating over this weekend. If either party saw the legislation, they may decide that that would be better for them than actually negotiating.
We are holding off looking at the legislation, but we are willing to commence second stage reading if the minister finds that it is necessary.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ACT TO PROVIDE FOR THE CONTINUATION OF POSTAL SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my colleague has reflected the consensus that was reached among the various parties. But just to be crystal clear, which I am sure the minister would want all members to be, we would concur with commencing the second reading of the bill in question on Monday.
However, if the parties are progressing with the various outstanding items and the parties so indicate to the minister and to the respective representatives of the party, I do not believe it would be necessary to proceed with the legislation on Monday.
In fact it would perhaps be inappropriate to proceed while negotiations are progressing. The minister should clearly understand that we would have to deny forthwith all stages of the bill on Monday but would be prepared to commence second reading on Monday if in fact the parties in the postal dispute indicate that there has been a breakdown and no possibility of resolving the dispute.

Mr. Speaker, in that case, I would like to table the following motion:

October 25, 1991
Business of the House

That, notwithstanding any Standing Order and usual practices of this House, on Monday, October 28,1991 at 12 p.m., the House shall proceed with the daily routine of business under the heading Introduction of Government Bills and that a bill placed on the Order Paper on October 23, 1991 in the name of the Minister of Labour entitled an act to provide for the continuation of postal service be introduced, read a first time and deemed printed;
That immediately thereafter the House proceed under Government Orders with the debate at second reading of the said bill;
That this order shall be rescinded if the Minister of Labour or government House leader rises from their seat at any time during daily proceedings on a point of order and advises the House that the employer and employees of the postal service have come to a mutual agreement.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, you will find unanimous consent for this motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to participate in this debate on second reading of Bill C-35.
I want to say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, since you have been the one who raised the issue of co-operation from opposition members of Parliament, that Bill C-35 was discussed at House leaders' meetings. We did not believe that we would be proceeding with it today. In fact it was indicated quite clearly that we would be proceeding with the motion with regard to conflict of interest.
However, the government has the right to change the agenda, which it has in this particular instance, and the minister quite rightly has alluded to the chronology of events surrounding the contents of Bill C-35.
The bill itself is a miscellaneous bill affecting a good number of statutes which I will read into the record momentarily. However, I wish to inform members that this is kind of an unusual procedure, unusual in the sense of previous occasions when a miscellaneous statute of this particular magnitude has come forward as it has in previous Parliaments and sessions. It has been customary that there would be a pre-study of the bill by members of Parliament so thereafter, when the minister would come into the House and ask to go to Committee of the Whole, leave would be granted. When he would ask to go on to report stage, third reading, to wrap the bill up, co-operation was always forthcoming.
That is the way it has operated in the past but that is not the way it is operating today.
We have indicated that we would not be able to proceed with this particular bill today, but nevertheless the government has decided to stick with its agenda and bring forward this particular bill.
The bill deals with numerous technical amendments to more than 90 statutes that cover-

This is a breach of the traditions of this House. Mr. Speaker, I am sure you would want me as an individual and as an opposition House leader to stand in this place and attempt to support the important traditions of this House, which we believe to be very important.

Section 9, headed the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act, says:
9.	The heading preceding section 21 of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
And then:
10.	Subsections 21(2) and (3) of the said Act are repealed and the following substituted therefor:
(2) The President shall, on or before September 15, 1993 and every five years thereafter, submit to the Minister a comprehensive report, in addition to the annual report of the Agency, providing an evaluation of all activities in which the Agency was involved and the impact those activities have had on regional disparity.
I am somewhat surprised when I hear the Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, the Minister of Public Works from Central Nova, and the Minister of Employment and Immigration from the province of New Brunswick refer to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency as being-as they say in news reports and in their public musings with small business and everyone elsethe panacea to correct the regional inequalities and disparities within the region.
I have to ask myself if it is such a positive vehicle for positive change why do you only want to tell us every five years? Why would you not want to tell us every year about the wonderful workings, the tremendous contribution of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency? Why? Why would you wait five years? Perhaps the minister cannot prepare a report on an annual basis. There is an annual report. I will read the bill again for your understanding, Mr. Speaker, because I know that you are as concerned as I am with the efficiency and effectiveness of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. The bill says:
The President shall, on or before September 15, 1993 and every
five years thereafter, submit to the Minister a comprehensive report,
in addition to the annual report of the Agency.

Mr. Speaker, did you hear that? One of my colleagues said: Perhaps the reason why they would not want to do it, say every second year or every third year, is that they do not have anything positive to report.
That would be very different. That is very different from what we are hearing from the Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and the Minister of Public Works. I do not know who to believe.
I want to say that I am leaning very heavily toward the comments of my colleague who happens to reside in the great province of Prince Edward Island.
I am leaning. I might get there. I might have a conclusion which will be obvious to each and every one of us in the House.
Just the other day the 1991 annual report of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency was released and it said: "During 1990 the economy of the Atlantic provinces hosted a surprisingly good performance, despite the recession". Wasn't that wonderful? I did not hear from the minister. I did not hear from the member for Central Nova.
I want to talk about the member for Central Nova, the Minister of Public Works, because he is a leading figure in Nova Scotia politics. He is a dear and close personal friend of the premier of Nova Scotia, the hon. Don
October 25, 1991

Cameron. They have done a phenomenal job in the province of Nova Scotia.
Unemployment in many regions of Nova Scotia is at an unprecedented high level. Youth unemployment is at an unprecedented high level. The Lingan mine in my own district is closing down. The port of Halifax and centres for women are closing down. Workers at Sydney Steel have no bridge programs in order to benefit them and their families who are suffering as a result of lay-offs. That has been a dismal performance by the hon. member for Central Nova. He ought to be ashamed of himself, for allowing this kind of gobbledegook about the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency while sitting in the federal cabinet.
I say that because the member for Central Nova, the Minister of Public Works, was the former Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. Imagine saying "a surprisingly good year" as if there were no problems in Atlantic Canada. Bankruptcies were revealed today and 56,000 Canadians have had to file for bankruptcy in this country. I am surprised, if we are doing so well with the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, that the government would have to wait for five years to give a comprehensive report telling the people of Atlantic Canada what a great job it has been doing for Atlantic Canada.
In my view the ministers and officials at ACOA have glossed over the the disturbing economic statistics in the period covered by its own annual report which shows that high interest rates and the high dollar policy of this government are dragging down the regional economy. There are significant increases in bankruptcies, higher unemployment throughout the region, startling declines in growth in forestry related industries, and an over-all decline in investment expenditures. That is the reality.
I am trying to discuss the public relations of the Government of Canada which it tries to slip into Bill C-35. We are told in Atlantic Canada, as my colleague from Charlottetown would gladly attest and support, that this agency, the panacea for rectifying regional disparities in this country, is doing a phenomenal job. In the legislation, tucked in with 90 other federal statutes, it
Government Orders
says that the government is only going to give the people a comprehensive report every fifth year.
Perhaps there may be an election in that period of time which we on this side look forward to with great anticipation, as I am sure members opposite also look forward to it. This agency, which will now make a comprehensive report in accordance with this particular statute every five years, has had some very dismal failures. It has had some successes but to suggest and imply that this particular agency has fulfilled its stated legislative mandate is beyond comprehension and is not acceptable to those of us who live in Atlantic Canada.
This agency has been approached by numerous groups for funding only to find that the criteria has changed. Its agencies in many parts of the Atlantic region have been a dismal failure.
The hon. member opposite, who is in the Chamber today, may disagree with what I say. I can well understand that. The fact of the matter is that the four Atlantic premiers, including the Tory premier of the province of Nova Scotia who happens to be the dear friend of the minister from Central Nova, have all concluded that the effectiveness of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency is certainly not what the ministers who sit on the benches opposite, representing Tory ridings in Atlantic Canada, have been telling the people in that region.
We have gross, and I underline the word gross, unemployment in Atlantic Canada. The fisheries industry is on its knees. Employees of the steel industry have had to resort to what many have termed civil disobedience to get any kind of attention whatsoever from the powers that be both at the provincial and federal level. The Atlantic premiers, one of them a Tory, have all commented on the ineffectiveness and the major shortcomings of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency.
When I read "every five years" and then hear the ministers say that it is the panacea, I say to myself: "That is double talk at its best. Perhaps some would even say hypocrisy at its best". I would not say that, but there are individuals in Atlantic Canada who would say that it is hypocrisy at its best.
This is a sham. What the Government of Canada is trying to do to those of us in the Atlantic region through Bill C-35 is a sham.

I have read the recent speech of the president of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency where he talked about the importance of tourism. Those of us who reside in the Atlantic region and those of us who represent constituencies in the Atlantic region know full well that tourism in P.E.I., Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland is indeed an important aspect of our economy. I would hope that when the comprehensive report is tabled before Parliament on the fifth anniversary thereafter in 1993, it would clearly spell out what the GST and the proliferation of the Tory taxes have done for tourism in Atlantic Canada. Individual operators in Atlantic Canada, whether they operate a motel, a small restaurant or some other commercial enterprise, will clearly say that the proliferation of almost 32 Canadian taxes by the government opposite, along with the GST, has taken a terrible toll on those operators in Atlantic Canada.
Tourism is down significantly among private operators and private entrepreneurs in my own region in Atlantic Canada, according to the Cape Breton Tourism Association. Jobs are fewer, the investments are down and the infrastructure is down. There is a substantial gap in the Atlantic economy.
I underline the significance of what we are debating here today. It is very important that these things be brought to the attention of Mr. Speaker and to members of the House.
I have countless constituents, and I know of many others, in Atlantic Canada who have come forward to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency to seek funding and assistance, only to be turned down for a variety of reasons because they do not fall within the criteria. The criteria have changed. I am sure that the president of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency has said that the criteria have changed because we have done consultations and our constituents have asked for that. I think in part that is correct, but the fact of the matter is that ACOA, as the leading federal institution in Atlantic Canada for economic development, has not been fulfilling its mandate to the people of Atlantic Canada.
Tourism is one example. You cannot operate in isolation. You cannot have ACOA providing small sums of moneys to small businesses in that region of the country
on the one hand and then on the other hand the Minister of Finance, through the proliferation of taxes, draining Canadian citizens in that particular region. This makes it very unfavourable for Canadians to travel domestically to that region or indeed other regions of the country. I think of western Canada and in particular our neighbours to the south.
Now I understand. I understand why the government wants to give a comprehensive report only every fifth year. I understand, because what the minister says, what the ministers infer is very different from what is actually happening in Atlantic Canada. Is ACOA going to make a comment on transfer payments when they file in accordance with section 10 of Bill C-35? Is it going to comment in a comprehensive report in addition to the annual report of the agency, providing an evaluation of all activities in which the agency was involved and the impact those activities have had on regional disparity?
I will bet my bottom dollar that they are going to duck it. They are going to duck the issue. They do not want to stand up and talk about those programs of the Government of Canada and how the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency interfaces with those other agencies.
I will give another example. I talked about tourism. Let me talk about another one. Let me talk about unemployment insurance. This is a government that brought in Bill C-21. It told the people of Canada it was going to do all sorts of wonderful things. That has not materialized at all.
It told us in Atlantic Canada that the Government of Canada was moving out of the tripartite social contract that had been a fabric of Canada for a long time. The employee, the employer and the Government of Canada were all making contributions to the unemployment insurance fund which would be disbursed to individuals who through no fault of their own were either laid off or could not find meaningful employment.
The federal government has bowed out of that contract and has left the employees and the employers to themselves. We were promised in 1989 by the predecessor to the Minister of Finance that there would be no increases in the premiums for unemployment insurance. The fact is that the premiums went up 25 per cent. On January 1, 1992 they are going up another 5 per cent.

There are a good number of individuals out there who have commented. They now envisage that because of the job dislocation from the policies of this government and because of the high unemployment which will continue, other individuals will make applications for unemployment insurance. This will necessitate a further increase in premiums for the employer and the employee. It will further erode the confidence of small business in Atlantic Canada. It will cause further havoc to employees who are paying those premiums. The Minister of Finance could not give us a straight answer yesterday as to whether or not he would concur with an increase in the unemployment insurance premiums.
Will the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, which interfaces with all of the other agencies of the Government of Canada, give its comprehensive report? Will it speak to the issue of small business in Atlantic Canada and what its programs have done to small business in Atlantic Canada with the proliferation of the 32 taxes and the increase in the premiums for unemployment insurance? They cannot take it any longer.
If you are a motel operator in Souris, Prince Edward Island, if you own a restaurant in Glace Bay, if you have something in Restigouche, New Brunswick or in Comer Brook, Newfoundland, then that is a commercial enterprise. When you are a small business you are living from month to month or, still worse, from week to week. A further increase in premiums will cause undue significant harm to those small businesses which are operating. We all know because we have small businesses that are operating on a shoe string in every community in the country.
But, no, clause 10 of this bill says ACOA will report only every fifth year with a comprehensive report. I have to agree with those individuals in Atlantic Canada who from what the minister is saying in Atlantic Canada and from what this particular bill says call this hypocrisy. It is not fair or appropriate in the circumstances.
That is a second issue with respect to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency. If it is doing so well, why not ran to the finish line? Why not have the comprehensive report every second year to tell the people of Atlantic Canada what a fantastic job is being done?

Every year they are going to file an annual report. The annual report has some information in it. There is no question about that. The comprehensive report, as alluded to in this particular clause of Bill C-35, is of paramount importance to those of us who reside in Atlantic Canada.
I want to talk about another aspect of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency and the fact that it will be reporting every fifth year. Those of us who reside in Atlantic Canada understand that the role of the state cannot mean everything to everyone at any given time. We do understand that the state has a role to play. One of the things that we have argued vigorously and consistently is the fact that those of us in Atlantic Canada are without a significantly high quality public infrastructure to sustain the quality of life in Atlantic Canada and to urge economic opportunities in that region.
I take for example the province of New Brunswick. The province of New Brunswick has been making the request of the Government of Canada to participate in what we now know, and what we have known for a good number of years, is a renewed highway strengthening agreement. Roads, which are a basic tool of infrastructure, a basic tool of transportation, could be upgraded to meet the standards that we now understand to be important for 1991. But the Government of Canada and the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency said: "Our mandate really does not cover that. You will have to do that through a special agreement between the province and the feds".
It has never come about. They have been asleep at the switch. ACOA's response is: "That is not our mandate. That is not part of our function. We cannot do that. We do not have the wherewithal. We do not have the monetary sums to expend on this type of program".
I have been asking the federal government in co-operation with the provincial government to extend what is best known as the Fleur-de-lis trail. It is a very picturesque route in Nova Scotia which my colleague from Montreal, the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard who has visited with me on several occasions, has travelled on. Even he, although a colleague, had to admit that this was a very scenic route and there was an obligation certainly by the Government of Nova Scotia and the Government of Canada to provide money. I do not mean oodles and oodles of money, as the hon. member from Toronto would lead us to believe, but a sum of money

As a result they will have to go on welfare to provide some dignity and some semblance of respect for their families and themselves.
The Government of Canada and the Minister of Employment and Immigration have not been of any assistance in this regard. However in fairness to the federal government-and I want to be fair as I always am-it is the provincial government, Tweedledee, and the federal government, Tweedledum, who have not shown the initiative to put forward a package which would be of some assistance to those steel workers displaced at Sydney Steel. It is they who have fallen down. As my colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys has said time and time again, the Government of Nova Scotia is acting in concert with the federal government to deny Canadians in his constituency and throughout industrial Cape Breton the economic opportunity to provide for their families.
What is even more ridiculous is that the feds are going to pay anyway. They are going to pay anyway. Why? Because the feds contribute 50 per cent of the welfare costs. We are going to pay them the other way so why can the government not be somewhat creative, somewhat innovative and provide a work program. Many programs are needed in industrial Cape Breton, picturesque as it is.

This is one of the reasons I wanted to come to this place, to try to influence policies that would lead to lower taxes but there is more than trying to foster a tax revolt inside and outside of Parliament.

The release in 1986 of classified military documents has revealed decades of intentional and accidental release of airborne radioactive contamination which travelled throughout the Pacific northwest, including Canada.
Growing evidence of thyroid disease and elevated levels of thyroid and other cancers among populations exposed to the releases of radioactive 1-131 has prompted two U.S. studies. Here in Canada, B.C. medical authorities and the Canadian Medical Association have urged the Mulroney government to join these studies to determine the level of risk to Canadians. I would ask the Minister of Finance if he would clearly state for the purposes of small business and employees across this country that he will stick by the word of his predecessor and have no further increases in the premiums for unemployment insurance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my answer today is the same answer I gave in the House yesterday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on page 30 of the 1989 budget papers, his predecessor states, and I quote: "The government will continue to contribute to the financing of unemployment insurance in difficult economic times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums".
I ask the Minister of Finance again, will he give an assurance that he will stick to the decision and the comments made by his predecessor, as the Minister of Finance, and there will be no increases in the unemployment insurance premiums as indicated in that statement? Yes or no.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I repeat, the answer that I give in the House today is exactly the same answer that I gave in the House yesterday. If the hon. member wants to quote the former Minister of Finance he can quote the budget of February 1991 when he said, and I quote: "Rates will be adjusted in such a manner to ensure the financial integrity of the account".
That is what the Minister of Finance said in the budget of 1991 and that certainly applies, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Porter study said something that most of us have been saying for quite a long time, and that is that regional economic development should be based on local strengths.
My question is for whomever is speaking on behalf of the minister responsible for ACOA, which has had a number of large projects under RCMP investigation over the past year. Now it stands to lose another $4 million in another patronage-ridden deal. This is the result of High Tech Woodworkers which went bankrupt after three months of operation and now has been sold for $1.2 million.
My question is as follows: Is it not about time that this government started building on local economic strengths to produce permanent jobs rather than local patronage to produce bankruptcies?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that the hon. member sounds very clever in making that statement. Surely, if he was correct in his facts his conclusion would certainly be correct as well.
There have been a number of risks taken in trying to develop Atlantic Canada, which is the purpose for which ACOA was created. Its success rate is pretty high nevertheless. The rate of failures is about 5 per cent out of 100. There were a number of failures in the Cape Breton area, all of which was acknowledged. There was a report done in connection with the situation by Mr. Anthony Brait. The agency has been re-evaluated since then and a report done by the Moncton economist,

whose name escapes me for the moment. You all know the name that I am seeking. We are following the recommendations of those reports and in Cape Breton in particular we want to concentrate more on smaller enterprises and on ideas and suggestions that come from within the region, rather than from without.
So, mistakes have been made and-Oh, give me a chance, I haven't been here for three or four days.
It certainly shows.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. minister may be able to jog his memory while we listen to the supplementary.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of State for Science and Technology.
The Porter report also criticizes the government for its research and development policy. Now we hear that the government is about to kill Canada's participation in the international fusion project.
My question is this: Given the great potential of this project to produce long-term environmentally sustainable energy, and given that Canada could be a likely site to receive $1.5 billion in benefits by virtue of the establishment here of the thermonuclear plant, does cutting this $13 million really make sense, I ask you, when we are spending hundreds of millions of dollars on TRIUMF-KEAON and hundreds of millions of dollars on a space project that will not produce nearly the benefits that this could potentially produce for Canada and the world?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member asked the question, and especially for his interest in fusion and the nuclear industry and his strong support for that industry.
I am pleased that the party has had a change of view since the questions were received yesterday. I simply say to the hon. member that the Minister of State for Research and Development and Treasury Board are looking at this project and Canadian involvement in it. I
Oral Questions
thank him for his support and I am glad also that he is going to make these representations to his party and his leader.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the president of Canada Post was appointed by Privy Council Order 435, of which I have a copy, in 1986, for five years up to this year, at a salary "within the range $165,000 to $205,000". That expired on February 17 of this year and in March of this year, a month later, the Privy Council listed his new salary range from $248,000 to $310,000, not counting his bonus.
Does the minister not find this a little difficult to digest, awarding a 50 per cent salary increase to the president of Canada Post so quickly, so quietly, and telling the rest of Canadians to accept zero per cent and tighten their belts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when Don Lander took over as president of Canada Post the taxpayers of Canada were contributing by way of subsidy hundreds of millions of dollars, $500 million a year.
In the last two years under Don Lander's presidency, Canada Post has returned to the taxpayers, to the Consolidated Revenue Fund, almost $200 million by way of dividends.
I understand that the hon. member does not think that a man with that kind of accomplishment should get paid as much as some third string second baseman, but frankly the taxpayers of Canada have got terrific value for the money we have paid Don Lander in salary. We as trustees of the taxpayers of Canada should be applauding him and wishing that the other leaders in our economy were as productive as him.

Madam Speaker, this government has closed post offices, replaced postmasters and postmistresses with outdoor boxes that freeze up in the winter time and in the interest of profit has destroyed our postal service in many ways.

October 25, 1991
Oral Questions
Will this government return our postal service to its original purpose, to deliver the mail quickly and fairly to all Canadians, and will the minister now roll back Mr. Lander's salary to at least a measly quarter of a million dollars a year and tell him that he is not going to get his Christmas bonus this year for being a good boy last year?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member is saying we should go back to the past when taxpayers dipped into their pockets to subsidize the post office $500 million to $600 million. We are still paying interest on those subsidies we had to borrow the money for in the past. I certainly would not recommend we return to the bad old past in that context.
The international postal union says that Canada Post is the most efficient postal system in the world. Surveys by independent market survey companies of the changes the post office has implemented in terms of new outlets in comer grocery stores and so on show a 90 per cent approval rating.
No, we are not going to go back to the past. Come on, George, join the present and the future.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Tory government gave the president of Canada Post a salary increase of $131,250. Meanwhile, Huguette Perrier, a 65 year old widow, who has delivered mail in Dalkeith, Ontario in my riding for nine years, was fired to save Canada Post $1,500 a year. Is that justice?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the unanimous consent of all sides of the House, in 1981 the member for Papineau introduced a bill creating a Crown corporation and we all agreed in this House that the corporation should run like a business and should operate at arm's length from the government. It was unanimously agreed. In terms of remuneration of senior officials in Crown corporations and agencies, we have an outside group that advises us on what is appropriate given the marketplace and the salary
levels. That group, as a matter of fact, was set up by the Liberal government.
Is the hon. member suggesting we go back to the bad old days where all of these decisions as to who is delivering mail here are done on a partisan basis and are done by the politicians, or should be accept the judgment of this House in 1981 to let the post office operate at arms length, and should we not be applauding the fact that it is now the most efficient post office in the world.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if I were this government I would not talk about nominating people on a partisan basis.
This has to do with fairness again. How can a government give the head shogun of Canada post a $131,250 salary increase and fire someone who delivers the mail in my riding, a widow, to save $1,500? Is that not at least wrong in the eyes of the minister or is there no sense of fairness at all left with this government?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
As I tried to explain to the hon. member this government, in following the instructions of this House, does not get involved in the individual decisions of the post office as to how to deploy its staff, which businesses to open, and so on. That was the instruction from the House. We are following those instructions.
The hon. member is suggesting, presumably, that these decisions as to who is hired or fired are made by politicians. People would call that a patronage-based system. I do not think that is appropriate.
The question of the service to people and the management of the post office has been examined and assessed by independent pollsters. We have the track record. I think it is absurd for anybody to look at that record and suggest we go back to the bad old days when taxpayers had to dip into their jeans to subsidize an inefficient operation. We should be applauding-

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, farmers in Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta, and Saskatchewan recently held large rallies to demonstrate their opposition to the government's agricultural programs and policies. Those farmers, including 7,500 in Regina last night, have said very loudly and clearly that there are deficiencies with the GRIP and NISA programs and that funds available under the so-called third line of defence must be increased.
In light of this protest, is the government prepared to acknowledge the farmers' growing plight? Will the government take steps to correct the obvious deficiencies in GRIP and NISA? Will the government increase the funds available under the third line of defence?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member knows, GRIP is a tripartite arrangement that involves the provinces, the federal government and the producers. I want to remind the hon. member that payments are being made under both the NISA program and GRIP.
As a matter of fact and to put it on the record, Madam Speaker, some $548 million was to be paid by September 15 in the form of the emergency assistance which was announced this spring. There is roughly $1.5 billion to be paid between now and the end of the year under the interim payments under the GRIP program, plus the
Oral Questions
$800 million that will be paid out as soon as possible over this year and next year. That totals something in the order of $3.4 billion. If you subtract the producers' premiums of $536 million, there will be something in the order of $2.8 billion flowing to the agricultural community between now and the end of June. While they do not have that money in hand at the present time, these funds are being processed and/or being mailed.
I am sure that will be very helpful in farmers meeting their debt obligations and planning for the future.

supplementary, Madam Speaker. Seven thousand, five hundred farmers in Regina last night were very much aware of the money that the government has provided and they have said it is not enough.
I hope the government is listening to those 7,500 plus hundreds of thousands of others out there.
The calls for a deficiency payment have been voiced since spring. The money has been needed for months, yet it appears that the government's intention for the third line of defence payout will not come until some time in 1992.
Given that the money is needed immediately, is the government prepared to advance those funds now to meet the needs expressed so strongly last night in Regina?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as the hon. member knows, in the spring we announced an emergency program of something in the order of $600 million. This $800 million deficiency payment is in addition to that and in addition to the payments that will be made out under the NISA and GRIP programs.
I remind the hon. member that between now and spring seeding, there will be something in the order of $2.8 billion or $2.9 billion net flowing to the farmers of Canada.
The hon. member suggests that is not enough. I think that $2.8 billion is a heck of a lot of money. In addition, we note that yesterday's Statistic Canada forecast indicates that farm income will be up by 10 per cent. We are expecting that there will be a further advance of credit to the Soviet Union which will probably result in an additional $400 million to $500 million worth of grain

sales, a good portion of that which will be shipped in this calendar year. So there will be cash flow and there will be deliveries made.
The money is either in the process of being mailed or in the process of being calculated. I ask the hon. member to tell his producers that money is on the way. As far as the $700 million or $800 million that was announced, we will provide it as soon as we possibly can.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Some time ago, the government announced that in January 1992, businesses would no longer be able to deduct the provincial payroll tax from their federal income tax. This is crazy! And all because the government has a difference of opinion with a number of provincial governments. Madam Speaker, this is an incredible act of discrimination against Quebec businesses that create jobs. Why the cut throat approach?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is simply to stop the erosion of the federal tax base and the hon. member I am sure would appreciate that.
There are ongoing discussions with the province of Quebec. The hon. member should realize that if this were allowed to continue right across the board, the federal tax base would be totally eroded. We want to try to work this thing out as amicably as we possibly can. Discussions are currently under way to ensure that this can be resolved in a satisfactory manner.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the minister responsible for Montreal. This tax clearly discriminates against Quebec, which will pay half the $7 million it will raise. This tax will bankrupt businesses and throw people out of work.
The minister says he defends Montreal, so why did he accept a tax that will further increase unemployment in a city where the unemployment rate is already over 13 per cent? How many more Angus plants will have to close before he understands?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour

That is what we intend to do, and with the revenue we collect, we will be in an even better position to help Montreal.

7,000	farmers gathered in Regina yesterday. They expressed on their own behalf and on behalf of thousands of others the concerns of Canadian farmers.

There are payments going out under the NISA program and as soon as we can get a decision from the third line of defence committee as to what is the
October 25, 1991

most appropriate way of distributing the $800 million, we will be in a position to start putting that in place. All I can say to the hon. member is that we will try to get the money flowing as quickly as we possibly can, provided we can find it, and as the hon. member knows, that is still a very difficult task. However, we understand the urgency and the plight out there and I know it is shared by the hon. member. We are going to do it as quickly as we can.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary is to the Deputy Prime Minister as well. As he knows, there are many ways we can assist the agrifood industry.
One year ago, the pesticide review committee submitted its report. No action has been taken to implement the recommendations of that report. Every time we ask, we are told "soon", "be patient", "it is coming", "it will be here shortly". Another year has gone by and the positive effects that can have for the industry should and could have taken place last year.
I ask the minister: when will the recommendations of that report be put into place?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as the hon. member knows, the pesticide review committee was a very delicate initiative that had to balance both the concerns of the environmentalists and the environmental situation as well as agriculture and other elements. I think the committee did an excellent job in doing the study and coming forth with some very specific recommendations. It certainly is the intention of the government to implement those recommendations. I am not sure of the reason for the delay, but I will undertake to make those representations to the Minister of Agriculture on his return and get back to the hon. member as soon as possible.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Retailers have suffered a $15 billion drop in retail sales in August. This is clearly reflected in the latest bankruptcy figures which show an increase nationally of 38 per cent for the month of September and a devastating increase of 62 per cent in Atlantic Canada.
What is this government going to do to inject some confidence into the retail sector?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the September figures clearly show a little different trend.

Routine Proceedings
The August figures to which the hon. member has referred showed a rather substantive decline in automobile sales. That really affected the old retail sales figures.
If she will look at the September figures, she will note that automobile sales have increased by some 11 per cent. While sales have not recovered completely, it does not paint as dismal a picture in September as it did in August. In some respects the August figures have been overtaken by those in September where there has been an increase in automobile retail sales in the order of 11 per cent.
I should say as well that another good indicator is that housing resales are continuing to climb. Housing starts have shown a 19 per cent increase in the third quarter over the second quarter, which I believe is a reflection of the reduction in interest rates. Housing starts are in the order of 181,000 on an annualized basis.
Those are the indicators that I think are very important. I should say that the reduction in interest rates reduces the monthly payment for a person holding a $100,000 mortgage by about $300. That is going to be extra cash in the hands of consumers which they will be able to spend and I think that will revitalize the retail sector.

-Establish future needs and define standards for the Canadian primary highway system.
-Establish benefits and costs of meeting these needs.

which units were posted to Greece during wartime (b) which of those units seeing action in Greece received combat support from units of the Greek Resistance (c) are those members of the Greek Resistance who assisted Canadian combat units currently receiving financial assistance from the government (d) are members of Resistance forces from other Axis countries currently receiving financial assistance from the government?
Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House
of Commons): I am informed by the Department of National Defense and Veterans Affairs as follows:
a)	No Canadian Army units were posted to Greece during the Second World War.
b)	Not applicable.
c)	Since 1930, with the inception of the WVA Act, Allied Veterans have been eligible for War Veterans Allowance.
War Veterans Allowance is a form of social assistance available to veterans and their dependants who are in financial need. To qualify, a person must have the required war service and also meet age, health and income requirements. The purpose of this program is to ensure that, in recognition of war service, qualified individuals are provided with a regular monthly income to meet basic needs.
In 1985, the Federal Court of Canada ruled in favour of recognizing members of the Greek Resistance as members of the forces of His Majesty's allies or powers associated with His Majesty. Based on the Federal Court's ruling the War Veterans Allowance Board formally recognized members of the Greek Resistance as Allied Veterans.
d)	To date there are 3 persons who served with the Italian Resistance movement during World War II receiving Veterans Affairs Canada benefits.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
subtopic: MISCELLANEOUS STATUTE LAW AMENDMENT ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, just before Question Period I had an opportunity to start putting a few comments on the record about Bill C-35, and I would like to continue now with them.
As you know, Madam Speaker, what we are dealing with in the House today is a bill with quite a title that I think Canadians would be interested in:
An act to correct certain anomalies, inconsistencies, archaisms and errors in the Statutes of Canada, to deal with other matters of non-controversial and uncomplicated nature therein and to repeal certain provisions thereof that have expired or lapsed or otherwise ceased to have effect.
The legislation, which is being brought before us today, is a mouthful for us to consider. These are essentially a number of changes to government legislation that are, in the government's hopes anyway, deemed non-controversial and that should not have any debate.
I did say, at the opening of my comments, that when the minister who introduced the bill first spoke he said that he was hoping to get unanimous consent in the House to move as quickly as possible today into Committee of the Whole to consider this bill. I said at that time, and I repeat it now, that our party cannot give that unanimous consent.
I think that is an important point to make. A bill of some 120 pages that amends a large number of statutes should be given an opportunity for a closer examination in committee. That is only appropriate.
We are quite prepared at this stage of the debate to move along quickly. But it is only proper that this Parliament, when considering a bill like this, has a closer examination of the bill in committee to see just what is in there.
Certainly, when this House receives a report from the legislative committee, we will be more than prepared to give the legislation its consideration and its early passage.
Why do I say that we have to do this, Madam Speaker?
I have not been a member of Parliament for a very long time but I have had an opportunity over the past to see what other governments have done, including this government, when we are presented with these omnibus bills. When you start going through these bills you have a number of questions. As a member of Parliament I do

Government Orders
not think that I would be serving my constituents or my country if I did not look closely at this legislation to ensure that we did not pass a stinker.
We have had that in British Columbia. The Social Credit government had quite a tradition. At the end of the session, when the legislature would be rising shortly and there is an eagerness to pass legislation, along would come an omnibus bill. Only later do we find out exactly what a particular bill did, what it eliminated or destroyed or changed. I think it is important for us to give close examination but we are also prepared to give a fairly quick one.
I would just like to point out a couple of parts of this bill that give reason for this examination in committee before we pass it through this House. For example, on page 12a of the bill there is an amendment to the Canadian Environmental Protection Act which my interpretation would lead me to believe that we are reducing the authority and control that the government and the minister may have regarding toxic substances. That is an example where we certainly need the background material and comments from the government.
As well on page 13 there are questions of exporting and importing toxic substances. The question is whether this is a reduction in the authority of the government to take a look at the export or import of these dangerous products.
Another one, on page 15a, concerns amendments to the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act. My interpretation of the interpretation is that the regulations the government would lay out in licences, and I quote: "-need not be prescribed by regulation". It is certainly my view that we have to follow due process and ensure that when the Government of Canada does issue a licence the minister does not just write something on a napkin and say: "It is okay and off you go". There is a process that we follow, the Order in Council process and gazetting, which is important for us to consider.
There is one part of the bill that is a positive change, which I think we could support. It is the addition of a clause which says: "This amendment which would add the underlined words would permit the drafting of legislation using feminine pronouns". All too often it is "he" will do this and "he" will do that. I think it might be a refreshing change for the government across the way if
"she" were to do this or "she" were to do that. Of course it would refer to a minister generally, male or female. That is a positive change which we should have in this legislation.
Another one is a new amendment on page 37a. This is an amendment to the Parliamentary Employment and Staff Relations Act:
This amendment will ensure that adjudicators can summon and
enforce the attendance of witnesses.
Without seeing the rest of that act the question I have concerns legal representation. Often people ask that lawyers represent them. Does this deal with that section at all?
As well, on page 42a under the Statistics Act there would appear to be an amendment that will allow Statistics Canada to start sharing information with other departments, municipalities, or other corporations. The amendments here lay out how that is to be done. My concern is how the public is to know if Statistics Canada starts sharing a lot of information with Visa or MasterCard or goodness knows any other mailing list that people might be on.
My point is that I do not think it is a proper procedure for this House to be asked to go into Committee of the Whole immediately when we know that given the pressure of time we will be asked to pass this legislation without giving it the consideration and thought that is needed.
That is why we will be refusing the consent of the government to rush this through. I think there is reason enough to send it to committee, not to spend a lot of time in committee, but reason enough to give it some thought in committee so that when it is reported back to the House we will hear from all members of the House on that committee whether this bill on the whole is worth supporting. We will then know if there are some concerns about this legislation which require amendments, and we can then allow the rest of the bill to pass.
To wrap up, we are prepared to move this bill quickly into committee. That is where it has to go as far as we are concerned, but we are not going to give it the old legislative rush. We will certainly welcome comments from the government in due course. Then the legislation and some of the good points I have mentioned can be
October 25, 1991

passed, and concerns about parts of the bill can be addressed.

Madam Speaker, I rise to add my comments to this proposed legislation and to help rush it through the House. In another motion here today I believe we are talking about the decorum and the way we do things in this institution.
I believe, as our House leader, the House leader of the New Democratic Party and other members of the other party have said, that we cannot bring this type of legislation in at the last minute and rush it through without more scrutiny. Routine Proceedings

We on this side of the House do not believe that we should do that at this time. In all sincerity I say that we are looking later in the day to make this place a better one in which to serve. I am all for that. I said that the other day.
